% =====================================================================
\begin{abstract}
\noindent This study answers two research questions about $n \times n$ matrix
multiplication under a strictly sequential, single-language (C) protocol.
\emph{Part A} asks how two classic optimisations---$i$-$k$-$j$ loop
reordering and cache blocking---change the runtime and memory profile of the
validated triple-loop baseline of Assignment 1 on identical inputs
($n \le 3000$, float64). \emph{Part B} asks under which tested sparsity
conditions a custom compressed-sparse-row (CSR) implementation of Gustavson's
sparse-by-sparse product beats the best dense kernel on identical logical
inputs (densities from $50\%$ down to $0.1\%$). Every configuration uses one
warm-up run, five measured repetitions, a monotonic kernel-only timer, a
per-run watchdog of 120\,s and a named peak-resident-memory metric; medians
and interquartile ranges (IQR) are reported and every raw measurement is
published. \emph{Main findings:} (i) both optimisations reduce kernel time at
large $n$---by $10.8\times$ ($i$-$k$-$j$) and $18.1\times$ (blocking) at
$n = 2000$, with the gap widening once the working set exceeds the
last-level cache; (ii) the CSR product ranges from $\approx
1.5\times10^{4}$ faster than dense multiplication at $0.1\%$ density to
$\approx 1.7\times$ slower at $n = 200$, $50\%$ density, so the sparse
advantage is governed by $n$ and density jointly through the output
fill-in; (iii) the sparse storage advantage shrinks from $\approx 300\times$
to exact parity as the product densifies, but it never reverses at the
tested densities. Conclusions are scoped to the tested hardware,
implementations and inputs.
\end{abstract}

% =====================================================================
\section{Introduction and Objective}

Matrix multiplication is the canonical $O(n^3)$ dense kernel and the
canonical case study for both \emph{locality-driven} optimisation and
\emph{sparse} representations. Assignment 1 established a validated,
reproducible triple-loop baseline in C and showed its empirical growth on
this machine. Assignment 2 extends that study along the two axes required by
the course specification: algorithmic optimisation of the dense kernel
(Part A) and storage format for sparse inputs (Part B).

\subsection*{Research questions}
\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{RQ1 (Part A):} How do $i$-$k$-$j$ loop reordering and
    cache blocking affect the kernel time and peak memory of the validated
    $i$-$j$-$k$ baseline, for identical inputs, numeric type and timing
    boundary?
    \item \textbf{RQ2 (Part B):} For which tested density levels does a CSR
    (Gustavson) product outperform the best dense kernel on the \emph{same
    logical} sparse matrices, once conversion and output fill-in costs are
    accounted for?
\end{enumerate}

\subsection*{Hypotheses (declared before the measurements)}
\begin{itemize}
    \item H1: $i$-$k$-$j$ reordering will be faster at moderate-to-large $n$
    (unit-stride streaming of $B$ and $C$ in the innermost loop); at small
    $n$ the difference will be negligible because everything fits in cache.
    \item H2: cache blocking will beat plain $i$-$k$-$j$ at large $n$ by
    reusing panels of $B$ inside the cache; the gain depends on the block
    size and saturates once the panels no longer fit.
    \item H3: the CSR product will win by a large factor only at low
    density; the break-even density will decrease with $n$ because the
    product of two matrices with density $d$ has expected density
    $1-(1-d^2)^n$, which grows with $n$ (fill-in).
    \item H4: the peak resident memory of the sparse path will scale with
    $\mathrm{nnz}$ rather than with $n^2$, except that the sparse output $C$
    may make its storage exceed the dense $3 \times 8n^2$ bytes at high
    density.
\end{itemize}

% =====================================================================
\section{Background and References}

\subsection{Dense multiplication and data locality}
The triple loop computes $C_{ij} = \sum_{k} A_{ik} B_{kj}$ in $\Theta(n^3)$
arithmetic work \cite{horn2013}. The loop \emph{order} does not change the
operation count but changes which elements are touched while they remain in
cache: with $i$-$j$-$k$ the innermost loop reads $B$ column-wise (stride
$n$), causing one cache miss per element on matrices larger than the cache,
whereas with $i$-$k$-$j$ both $B$ and $C$ are streamed row-wise with unit
stride \cite{lam1991,goto2008}. Cache blocking (tiling) additionally
partitions the loops into panels so that working sets stay inside a chosen
cache level \cite{lam1991,goto2008,golub2013}. All dense kernels here
perform exactly the same floating-point work in the same accumulation order
per output element; only the traversal changes.

\subsection{Sparse storage and sparse-by-sparse products}
A CSR matrix stores $\texttt{rowptr}[0..n]$, $\texttt{col}[\texttt{nnz}]$
and $\texttt{val}[\texttt{nnz}]$, using $4(n+1) + 12\,\texttt{nnz}$ bytes
for float64 values \cite{davis2006,saad2003}. Gustavson's algorithm
multiplies two CSR matrices row by row: for row $i$ of $A$ it accumulates
$A_{ik} B_{k,:}$ into a dense workspace indexed by column, using a stamp
array and a linked list so that clearing costs only the touched columns;
the finished row is sorted to obtain canonical CSR \cite{gustavson1978}.
The product of two matrices with density $d$ is not sparse in general: under
an independent-Bernoulli model, $\Pr[C_{ij} \neq 0] = 1 - (1-d^2)^n$, so
for $nd^2 \gg 1$ the product is essentially dense (\emph{fill-in}); this
model serves only as an analytical reference---the measured
$\texttt{nnz}_C$ is always reported \cite{golub2013}.

\subsection{Floating-point determinism}
IEEE~754 addition is not associative \cite{ieee754}, so kernels that
traverse the operands in different orders may differ by small rounding
amounts; tolerances are declared in Section~\ref{sec:method}. The Gustavson
kernel accumulates each output element in a fixed $k$-order, making its
results bit-comparable across runs.

% =====================================================================
\section{Methodology}\label{sec:method}

\subsection{Implementations (custom student code in C)}
All kernels are custom C code under \texttt{src/c/}, share one storage
layout (contiguous row-major \texttt{double} arrays) and one uniform
contract: the kernel receives $A$, $B$ and a pre-allocated $C$ and must
produce $C = AB$ regardless of $C$'s previous contents; kernels that
accumulate zero $C$ \emph{inside} the timed region (an $O(n^2)$ cost against
$O(n^3)$ work), while allocation is always outside it. No value-dependent
shortcuts are allowed in the dense kernels, so arithmetic work is identical
for every dense method:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \texttt{dense\_ijk\_baseline} --- the validated Assignment 1
    triple loop (same code, flags and layout); it assigns $C_{ij}$, so it
    needs no zeroing.
    \item \texttt{dense\_ikj\_reorder} --- optimisation 1: loop order
    $i$-$k$-$j$; the innermost loop streams rows of $B$ and $C$ with unit
    stride and is auto-vectorised by GCC.
    \item \texttt{dense\_blocked} --- optimisation 2: tiled $i$-$k$-$j$
    with block size $b$; $b = 512$ is the default, justified by the tuning
    sweep in Table~\ref{tab:block-tuning}. For $n < b$ the kernel
    degenerates to plain $i$-$k$-$j$.
    \item \texttt{sparse\_csr\_gustavson} --- Part B: custom CSR
    structures plus Gustavson's row-wise SpGEMM with a dense accumulation
    workspace, stamp array and linked list; each output row is sorted by
    column index. The $O(n)$ workspace and the geometric growth of the
    output arrays are allocated inside the timed kernel and freed before it
    returns (documented boundary).
    \item \texttt{dense\_to\_csr\_conversion} --- timed separately (never
    mixed into the kernel comparison): triplet gather + sort + scatter.
\end{itemize}

\subsection{Inputs}
\textbf{Part A} reuses the exact Assignment 1 matrices (\texttt{A\_n.csv},
\texttt{B\_n.csv}; float64, uniform in $[-10,10]$, Mersenne Twister
seed~42) from \texttt{assignment1/data/matrices}; the bundled generator
\texttt{scripts/generate\_matrices.py} reproduces them bit-identically.
\textbf{Part B} matrices are generated deterministically inside the
harness: each entry is exactly $0.0$ with probability $1-d$ and otherwise
uniform in $[-10,10]$, drawn from a 32-bit LCG ($s \leftarrow 1103515245\,s
+ 12345$) whose stream restarts from seed~42 for every configuration, so
zero patterns at a given $n$ are nested across densities; the dense and
sparse paths consume the \emph{same} generated matrices. Tested sizes:
Part A $n \in \{10, 50, 100, 200, 400, 800, 1000, 1500, 2000, 3000\}$;
Part B $n \in \{200, 500, 1000, 2000\}$ plus $n = 3000$ for
$d \in \{10\%, 1\%, 0.1\%\}$, with densities
$d \in \{50\%, 20\%, 10\%, 5\%, 1\%, 0.1\%\}$ (sparsity $= 100\%-d$).

\subsection{Environment}\label{sec:env}
\input{tables/table_env}

\subsection{Timing, repetitions and budgets}
The timer is \texttt{clock\_gettime(CLOCK\_MONOTONIC)} and measures the
\emph{kernel only}: input generation/loading and output allocation happen
outside the timed region; output initialisation happens inside it when the
kernel requires it. After every run the harness computes $\mathrm{tr}(C)$
as an anti-dead-code-elimination checksum. Each configuration runs $1$
warm-up (kept in the CSV as \texttt{repetition\_id = 0}, excluded from
statistics) and $N = 5$ measured repetitions; very small matrices
($n \le 50$) are multiplied in batches of $100$ and the time is divided by
the batch factor. A per-run watchdog of $120$\,s aborts runs that exceed
the declared budget; aborted runs are recorded with \texttt{status =
TIMEOUT} and \emph{no} execution time. The memory metric is the \emph{peak
process working set (RSS)} sampled every $5$\,ms by a background thread
(\texttt{GetProcessMemoryInfo}); as a sanity reference the analytic storage
of each representation is also reported (dense: $3\times 8n^2$ bytes;
sparse: CSR of $A$, $B$ and $C$ plus the $O(n)$ workspace). Sampled RSS and
analytic storage are different quantities and are never equated.

\textbf{Declared budgets.} Memory: 8\,GiB (the largest completed
configuration, $n = 3000$, needs $\approx 216$\,MB for $A$, $B$ and $C$;
no OOM occurred). Time: $120$\,s per run. The largest \emph{completed}
size differs per method because of this cap: both optimised methods finish
$n = 3000$, while the baseline's largest completed size is $n = 2000$ and
its $n = 3000$ warm-up is aborted by the watchdog (recorded as TIMEOUT).
The largest \emph{attempted} size is $n = 4000$ with the baseline kernel
($\approx 294$\,s per run in Assignment 1), recorded as a \texttt{TIMEOUT}
outcome in \texttt{data/results/results\_a2\_boundary.csv} without an
execution time.

\subsection{Correctness}
The harness refuses to benchmark unless the correctness gate passes:
identity and zero matrices, a known $2\times2$ product, every dense kernel
against an independent reference at $n = 33, 64, 65$; CSR round-trip
losslessness; Gustavson vs.\ dense product at four densities; and sparse
identity/zero products. Tolerances:
$\epsilon_{\text{abs}} = \epsilon_{\text{rel}} = 10^{-9}$. At benchmark
scale the harness compares the full result matrices of all executed methods
(maximum absolute difference logged in \texttt{crosscheck\_log\_*.csv});
for $n \le 3000$ the worst-case accumulation error
$n\,\epsilon_{\text{mach}}\,|C|_{\max} < 10^{-6}$, so cross-checks use
$\epsilon_{\text{abs}} = 10^{-6}$. A dumped baseline result is additionally
verified against \texttt{numpy.matmul} (NumPy is used only as a trusted
reference, never as a benchmarked method): at $n = 100$ the maximum
absolute difference is $6.82\times10^{-13}$ (PASS;
\texttt{data/results/numpy\_crosscheck\_log.txt}).

\section{Results}\label{sec:results}

All numbers below are computed by \texttt{scripts/analyze\_results.py} from
the raw CSVs in \texttt{data/results/}; every figure shows medians with
IQR-based variability, and memory values use the $2^{20}$-byte megabyte
convention of the harness.

\subsection{Part A: dense optimisation}

Part A produces a clean, size-dependent ordering of the three kernels
(Table~\ref{tab:dense-time}, Fig.~\ref{fig:dense-time}). For $n \le 100$
all three kernels run within $\approx 0.03$\,ms of each other (every median
is $\le 0.3$\,ms): the working sets fit in cache and the traversal order is
irrelevant. From $n = 200$ the optimised kernels are consistently faster
($1.35$--$1.73\times$ up to $n = 800$), and the gap grows with $n$: at
$n = 1000$ the medians are $\approx 982$, $434$ and $464$\,ms
($\approx 2.3\times$ and $2.1\times$); at $n = 1500$, $\approx 4.19$,
$1.72$ and $1.45$\,s ($2.4\times$ and $2.9\times$); at $n = 2000$,
$\approx 31.9$\,s (baseline), $2.96$\,s ($i$-$k$-$j$) and $1.76$\,s
(blocking)---$10.8\times$ and $18.1\times$ (these two ratios are the least
stable in the study: the baseline times at this size are bimodal, see the
anomalies note in the Discussion). At $n = 3000$ the baseline warm-up
exceeded the $120$\,s watchdog (\texttt{TIMEOUT}; its largest completed
size is therefore $n = 2000$), while $i$-$k$-$j$ needed $\approx 21.7$\,s
and blocking $\approx 11.6$\,s. The single baseline attempt at $n = 4000$
(largest \emph{attempted} size) was likewise aborted and carries no
invented time. The speedup ratios of Fig.~\ref{fig:dense-speedup} summarise
this trend: $\approx 1\times$ up to $n = 100$, $1.4$--$2.9\times$ for
$n = 200$--$1500$, and $10.8\times$/$18.1\times$ at $n = 2000$.

\subsection{Part B: sparse CSR vs.\ the best dense method}

Table~\ref{tab:sparse-time} summarises the 27 sparse configurations
(kernel times, conversion cost, input/output non-zeros and speedup over the
best dense kernel); Fig.~\ref{fig:sparse-speedup} plots the speedup versus
density. Five observations:

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \emph{The sparse advantage grows with $n$ and falls with
    density.} At $d = 0.1\%$ the sparse kernel is up to $\approx
    1.5\times10^{4}$ times faster than the dense kernel ($0.23$\,ms vs.\
    $3.42$\,s at $n = 2000$; $\approx 1.0\times10^{4}$ at $n = 3000$); at
    $d = 1\%$ the factor is $57$--$88\times$ depending on $n$.
    \item \emph{Break-even.} At $n = 200$ the sparse kernel loses down to
    $d = 10\%$ ($0.6\times$ at $50\%$: $3.15$ vs.\ $1.82$\,ms; $0.6\times$
    at $20\%$; $0.8\times$ at $10\%$) and wins from $d = 5\%$ down
    ($1.8\times$ at $5\%$, $58\times$ at $1\%$, $408\times$ at $0.1\%$),
    i.e., the break-even sits at $\approx 5$--$10\%$ density at this size
    (every $n = 200$ kernel median is $\approx 2$\,ms, i.e., in the noise
    regime discussed below). From $n = 500$ upward it is faster at
    \emph{every} tested density, including $d = 50\%$ (e.g., $n = 2000$:
    $2.20$\,s vs.\ $3.41$\,s, $1.6\times$; at $n = 500$ the margin is only
    $1.1\times$).
    \item \emph{Conversion} is measured separately and never mixed into
    the kernel comparison: across all configurations it ranges from
    $0.07$\,ms ($n = 200$, $d = 0.1\%$) to $300.6$\,ms ($n = 2000$,
    $d = 50\%$). At the lowest densities it exceeds the sparse kernel
    itself ($46\times$ at $n = 2000$, $d = 0.1\%$), yet the end-to-end
    sparse path (conversion $+$ kernel) still beats the dense kernel by
    $\approx 323\times$ there.
    \item \emph{Fill-in} (Fig.~\ref{fig:fill-in}): the measured
    $\texttt{nnz}_C$ (Table~\ref{tab:sparse-time}) tracks the
    independent-Bernoulli prediction $1-(1-d^2)^n$ closely: the maximum
    deviation of the output density over all $27$ configurations is
    $0.77$\,percentage points ($n = 200$, $d = 10\%$: $34\,334$ measured
    vs.\ $34\,641$ predicted non-zeros), and most points are far closer
    (e.g., $n = 1000$, $d = 5\%$: $919\,343$ vs.\ $918\,172$). The
    relevant predictor of the output density is $nd^2$, not $d$ alone.
    \item \emph{Memory} (Table~\ref{tab:memory-partb}): the theoretical
    storage of CSR($A$, $B$, $C$) never exceeds the dense $3\times 8n^2$ at
    the tested densities: it is \emph{exactly} equal at $d = 50\%$
    (fill-in makes $C$ dense, so
    $12(0.5 + 0.5 + 1)n^2 = 24n^2 = 3\times 8n^2$) and smaller everywhere
    else ($0.70\times$ at $d = 20\%$, $0.10\times$ at $d = 1\%$, and
    $\approx 300\times$ smaller at $d = 0.1\%$ for $n = 2000$). The
    sampled peak RSS column is a process-wide bound (see the limitations)
    and is reported for completeness, not as a per-representation measure.
\end{enumerate}

\section{Discussion}

\subsection{RQ1: what the two dense optimisations actually buy}
The evidence supports H1 and H2 with the predicted shape. The $i$-$k$-$j$
reorder changes only the traversal, yet it is $\approx 1.4$--$2.4\times$
faster from $n = 200$ to $n = 1500$ and $10.8\times$ at $n = 2000$: the
innermost loop streams rows of $B$ and $C$ with unit stride, which the
hardware prefetcher and the vectoriser can exploit, whereas the baseline
reads $B$ column-wise (stride $n$) and suffers one cache miss per element
once $A{+}B{+}C$ exceeds the last-level cache ($33$\,MB on this CPU: the
working set is $\approx 24$\,MB at $n = 1000$ but $\approx 96$\,MB at
$n = 2000$). Blocking adds panel reuse of $B$ across a block of rows, which
is why it ties plain $i$-$k$-$j$ within $\approx 10\%$ while everything
fits in cache ($n \le 1000$) but is $1.7\times$ faster at $n = 2000$ and
$1.9\times$ at $n = 3000$. The tuning sweep shows a clear clustering
($b \in \{256, 512, 1024\}$ agree within $\approx 10\%$ at
$n = 2000$--$3000$; $b \le 128$ is $1.4$--$2.3\times$ slower), itself
noisy at $n = 1500$ ($b = 32$: $900$\,ms vs.\ $b = 64$: $2122$\,ms,
consistent with the core-migration anomaly below). We therefore select
$b = 512$ as a representative of the best cluster rather than claiming a
precise optimum, and we do not claim it generalises to other CPUs. Memory
is unaffected by either optimisation, as required for a clean time
comparison.

\subsection{RQ2: where the sparse representation wins---and where it does not}
The percentage of zeros alone never determines performance; the outcomes
depend on $n$, on the \emph{output} structure and on whether conversion is
counted:
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{Work reduction, not storage, explains the high-density
    wins.} At $d = 50\%$ the product is completely filled by fill-in
    ($\texttt{nnz}_C = n^2$ at every tested $n$), so the sparse kernel has
    no storage advantage; it still wins for $n \ge 500$ ($1.1$--$1.6\times$)
    because Gustavson performs only the necessary
    $\mathrm{nnz}_A \cdot \overline{\mathrm{nnz\ row\ of\ B}} \approx
    0.125\,n^3$ multiply-accumulates instead of the dense $n^3$, and
    writes $C$ row by row. The per-row linked-list traversal and sorting
    are what make it lose at the smallest size ($n = 200$: $1.7\times$
    slower at $d = 50\%$, winning only from $d = 5\%$ down).
    \item \emph{Fill-in erodes, but never reverses, the storage
    advantage.} CSR($C$) costs $12$ bytes per non-zero, i.e.\ $1.5\times$
    the $8$ bytes of dense $C$, yet $A$ and $B$ become proportionally
    cheaper in CSR as $d$ falls: total CSR($A,B,C$) storage equals the
    dense $3\times 8n^2$ only at $d = 50\%$ and is smaller at every lower
    tested density ($0.70\times$ at $20\%$, $0.10\times$ at $1\%$, and
    $\approx 300\times$ at $0.1\%$ for $n = 2000$). H4's first part
    (storage scales with $\mathrm{nnz}$) is confirmed; its prediction that
    CSR storage \emph{exceeds} the dense layout at high density is refuted
    within the tested range---that would require $d > 50\%$.
    \item \emph{Conversion decides one-shot pipelines.} For repeated
    products of the same matrices the separately measured conversion is a
    one-off cost and the sparse kernel dominates. For a single
    multiplication it must be added: it is negligible against the dense
    kernel at all tested points, but it exceeds the sparse kernel itself at
    the lowest densities (absolute cost still small: $10.4$\,ms vs.\
    $0.23$\,ms at $n = 2000$, $d = 0.1\%$).
\end{itemize}
H3 is only partially confirmed: its first clause (large wins only at low
density) holds, but the predicted \emph{direction} of the break-even
density versus $n$ is refuted---the measured break-even \emph{increases}
with $n$ ($\approx 5$--$10\%$ at $n = 200$, above $50\%$ from $n = 500$
on), because the dense cost grows as $n^3$ while the sparse cost grows as
$d^2 n^3$ and the fixed sparse overheads matter only at small $n$. The
fill-in mechanism H3 invoked manifests in storage (H4, partially confirmed
above) rather than in time.

\subsection{Anomalies and limitations}
\begin{itemize}
    \item \emph{Run-to-run bimodality:} some configurations show two
    distinct time levels separated by a $\approx 1.4$--$2.1\times$ factor
    (baseline at $n = 2000$: $15.6$--$33.3$\,s; the dense kernel at
    $n = 500$ in Part B: $25.5$--$53.7$\,ms). The most plausible cause is
    the hybrid CPU ($8$ performance $+ 12$ efficiency cores): the
    single-threaded process is not pinned to a core type, so Windows may
    migrate it between runs. Thread counts were controlled, core \emph{type}
    was not. Medians and IQRs are reported; the qualitative conclusions
    rely on ratios $\ge 2\times$ that exceed this noise. Affinity pinning
    is planned for Assignment 3.
    \item \emph{Memory sampling:} the $5$\,ms RSS sampler cannot resolve
    peaks shorter than one sampling period; memory figures for the
    sub-millisecond configurations ($n \le 100$) are indicative only.
    Sampled RSS and analytic storage are different quantities and are
    reported separately. In addition, the Part B peak RSS of a kernel is a
    \emph{process-wide} bound: during cross-validation the harness holds
    both the dense and the CSR copies at once, and the allocator retains
    pages freed by earlier configurations of the same run (visible as the
    dense RSS growing across densities at a fixed $n$ in
    Table~\ref{tab:memory-partb}). Per-representation comparisons
    therefore use the theoretical storage columns only.
    \item \emph{Scope:} one machine, one compiler, one input family
    (uniform random values; random independent sparsity). Structured
    sparsity (banded, block, power-law) can produce very different fill-in
    and is out of scope. Part B dense baselines consume the same logical
    sparse inputs stored densely: they do not exploit sparsity, which is
    precisely the controlled contrast, not a defect. The $n = 4000$
    boundary was attempted only with the baseline kernel.
\end{itemize}

\FloatBarrier
% =====================================================================
\section{Conclusions}

Within the tested scope (single-threaded C, float64, one laptop CPU,
Assignment 1 baseline inputs and randomly sparse Part B inputs):

\begin{enumerate}
    \item \textbf{RQ1:} both optimisations reduce kernel time with zero
    memory cost and identical arithmetic. $i$-$k$-$j$ reordering yields
    $\approx 1.4$--$2.4\times$ up to $n = 1500$ and $10.8\times$ at
    $n = 2000$; cache blocking matches it within $\approx 10\%$ below
    $n = 1000$ and adds a further $1.7$--$1.9\times$ at $n = 2000$--$3000$,
    for a total of $18.1\times$ over the baseline at $n = 2000$ (the least
    stable ratio in the study, see the bimodality note). The block size
    must be tuned per microarchitecture ($b = 512$ here, a representative
    of the best cluster $b \in \{256, 512, 1024\}$; blocks $b \le 128$ lose
    $1.4$--$2.3\times$ at $n = 2000$). Under the declared $120$\,s budget
    the baseline cannot complete $n = 3000$ (TIMEOUT) while the blocked
    kernel needs only $\approx 11.6$\,s.
    \item \textbf{RQ2:} the custom CSR/Gustavson product is advantageous
    over a wide tested range: break-even against the best dense kernel lies
    at $\approx 5$--$10\%$ density at $n = 200$, but from $n = 500$ on the
    sparse kernel wins at every tested density---up to
    $\approx 1.5\times10^{4}$ at $n = 2000$, $d = 0.1\%$---even when
    fill-in makes the product fully dense (work reduction, not storage).
    The zeros percentage alone predicts nothing: the output density follows
    $1-(1-d^2)^n$, measured within $0.8$ percentage points, and CSR storage
    shrinks relative to dense storage as the product fills in---exactly
    matching it at $d = 50\%$ and never exceeding it at the tested
    densities. Conversion cost is negligible against the dense kernel at
    every tested point but dominates the sparse kernel at the lowest
    densities; it should be counted for one-shot multiplications.
\end{enumerate}

Open questions carried to Assignment 3: how these gains interact with
thread-level parallelism (does blocking still pay once cores share the
LLC?), whether affinity pinning removes the observed bimodality, and how
parallel sparse products behave under fill-in.

Assignment 1 dataset can be regenerated bit-identically with
\texttt{scripts/generate\_matrices.py}; every raw measurement of this study
is published in \texttt{data/results/} and every table/figure is regenerated
deterministically by \texttt{scripts/analyze\_results.py}. The complete
source code and data are publicly available in the project repository:
\url{https://github.com/TemiArtemi/MatrixMultiplicationBigData}.
